transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Um, what brings me in... gosh, it's a bit embarrassing to talk about, to be honest. I'm 55, you know, I work as a bookkeeping clerk, so I'm usually pretty organized, pretty by-the-book with my life. But lately, well, I've been taking this evening class to keep my skills sharp, and... well, what really pushed me to make this appointment is what happens after the class is over. 

I get out, and I'm just... I don't know, I'll stop for food on the drive home, which sounds normal enough, right? But I end up ordering and eating a completely full fast-food meal. And then, it's like a switch flips or something. I'll hit the vending machine and get a bunch of candy, just whatever is in there, and eat all of that too. And then I finally get home, and I'm still not done. I'll just keep going, tearing into more snacks at the house, just whatever I can find in the pantry or the fridge. 

It’s honestly like... it's like I am making up for the whole entire day all at once. I just sit there afterward looking at all the wrappers and I don't even know how it happened, but it just keeps happening after these evening classes, and I just... I really don't know what to do about it anymore. It's really been weighing on my mind.
Do you feel like you're in control of your eating during these episodes after class?

Control? No, no, that's exactly the problem, Doctor. I really don't have any control at all. It's... well, let me try to explain it properly. You know, like I said, I'm a bookkeeper, so my whole life is about control and making sure everything balances out perfectly. Everything has a column, everything has a place. But during these... these times after class, it's completely different. 

I'll get home, and I usually sit down at the kitchen island—sometimes I don't even bother turning on the main overhead lights, just the little one over the stove—and once I start on those snacks, it's like my brain and my body just disconnect from each other. I'll be sitting there, and I keep telling myself, 'Okay, that's enough now, just close the bag, put a clip on it, and go up to bed.' I mean, I know I have to be up early for work the next morning, and I know I don't need the food. But my hands... they just keep reaching for more. 

It's almost like I'm watching someone else do it. I just keep reaching into the bag, or opening another wrapper, and I can't stop. I'll just keep going and going until I feel so incredibly embarrassed and just... sick of myself. It's this terrible feeling, because normally I'm such a disciplined guy, you know? I pay my bills on time, I keep my house clean, but right then, sitting in the dark with all those wrappers, I just can't make myself stop no matter how hard I yell at myself in my head. I just keep eating until it's all gone.
Do you feel guilty after these eating episodes are over?

Guilty? Oh, gosh... yes. Guilty doesn't even begin to cover it, Doctor. It's this heavy, sinking feeling right in the pit of my stomach. Like I said, I'm a numbers guy, right? I calculate things. So I sit there, looking at the empty wrappers—the fast food bags, the candy wrappers from the vending machine, the empty chip bags from the pantry—and my brain just starts adding up the calories, the fat, the sheer volume of what I just put into my body. And the guilt is just... it's suffocating. 

I start thinking about my waistline, about how I'm 55 and my metabolism isn't what it used to be. I think about having to buy new trousers for work, going up a size, and how humiliated I'd feel. The fear of all that food just turning into fat and showing on me... it gets so overwhelming. And, well, I haven't told anyone this part, not a single soul, because it's just so shameful for a man my age... but a few times, maybe three or four times after those really bad late-night eating spells, the guilt and the panic got so bad that I... I went into the bathroom. 

I turned on the faucet so it would be loud, just in case, even though I live alone. And I stood over the toilet and I... I made myself throw up. I just couldn't bear the thought of all that food sitting inside me, ruining everything, making me gain weight. It's awful, it really is. I'd rinse my mouth out afterward and just stare at myself in the mirror, feeling even more pathetic than before. It's like a vicious cycle, you know? The eating makes me feel guilty, and the guilt makes me panic, and the panic makes me do... that. And then I just feel guilty all over again. I just want it to stop.
Do these episodes of eating happen when you're feeling stressed or anxious after the class, or is it more about the time of day or something else?

Well, that's... gosh, that's a really good question, Doctor. I've thought about that a lot, actually. You see, the class itself—it's an advanced Excel certification course, you know, macros and pivot tables, that sort of thing—it's not really stressful. In fact, I actually enjoy it. I like the logic of it, the way everything has a formula and a result. So I wouldn't say I'm leaving the class feeling anxious or worked up about the material. It's not like my mind is racing about spreadsheets when I get in the car. 

But as for why it happens then... I just don't really know. I've tried to analyze it, like I would a ledger that's out of balance. I look for the trigger, you know? Is it because it's late? The class ends at 8:30 PM, so by the time I'm driving, it's dark, the streets are quiet. Maybe it's just the fact that the day is over and there's this... this void, I guess? Or maybe it's just the routine of driving past that particular fast-food place on the way back. I've even tried taking a different route home, going down Elm Street instead of the main avenue, but then I just end up stopping at the gas station on the corner and buying snacks there instead. 

So, I can't really put my finger on it being stress, or anxiety, or even just the time of day. It's more like... it's just this thing that happens now. Like a bad habit that's taken on a life of its own. I sit in the car, the engine running, and I tell myself, 'Arthur, just drive straight home. You have chicken in the fridge.' But then my blinker goes on, and I'm pulling into the drive-thru, and I don't even fully understand why I'm doing it. I wish I had a better answer for you, I really do, because if I knew why it was happening, maybe I could figure out how to stop it. But right now, I'm just... I'm really at a loss.
Do you think these episodes of eating are triggered by any specific emotions you're feeling at that time?

Emotions... well, that's... I mean, I've really tried to sit down and parse it out, you know? Like I said, I like to balance the books, figure out where every cent goes, so I've tried to do that with my feelings, too. I've sat there with a cup of black coffee on a Sunday morning, just looking out the window at the neighbor's yard—they have this lovely oak tree that sheds leaves everywhere, which drives me a bit mad, but it's peaceful to look at—and I try to trace it back. I ask myself, 'Arthur, were you sad? Were you angry? Were you lonely?' 

And... honestly, Doctor, I come up empty. I really do. It's not like I'm sitting in the car crying over a lost love or fuming because my boss, Mr. Henderson, made a passive-aggressive comment about my filing system. It's not like that at all. It's almost an absence of emotion, if that makes any sense? It's just this... this blankness. I'm driving, the radio is on—usually just the local news or classical music, nothing that gets the blood pumping—and there's no big emotional wave crashing over me. 

I've read articles, you know, in those magazines at the dentist's office, about emotional eating. About people who eat a whole cake because they're heartbroken or stressed about a mortgage payment. But I just don't fit that mold. I don't feel a sudden spike of sadness or a sudden rush of anxiety right before I pull into the drive-thru. It's just... I'm driving, and then I'm eating, and the emotions—the terrible, overwhelming guilt and shame—they only show up *after* the fact. Beforehand? During? I really couldn't tell you that I'm feeling much of anything at all. It's incredibly frustrating not to have a neat little label to slap on it, like 'I eat because I'm sad.' I wish it were that simple.
Do you feel hungry when you start eating after the class?

Hungry? Well, gosh, you'd think so, wouldn't you? It would certainly make the whole thing a lot easier to understand if I were just, you know, famished. But... no. No, I'm really not hungry at all. I've actually paid close attention to that, because I thought, 'Arthur, maybe you're just not eating enough during the day.' But I always make sure to have a proper, sensible dinner before I even leave the house for the community center. Right around 5:30, I'll sit down and have a baked chicken breast, maybe some steamed carrots or a little side salad with a light vinaigrette. Very measured, you know? Just enough to keep the engine running. 

So by the time 8:30 rolls around and I'm driving home, my stomach isn't rumbling. There are no hunger pangs. I'm not lightheaded or anything like that. In fact, most of the time I can still physically feel that I'm perfectly satisfied from dinner. But then I'm in that drive-thru line anyway, and I'm ordering... well, I'm ordering enough food for three grown men. And when I start eating it—the burgers, the fries, all of it—it's not because my body is asking for nourishment. It's not a physical need for fuel. 

It defies all logic, really. If you look at it like a balance sheet, there's absolutely no deficit that needs filling. The account is already full, so to speak. I'm not eating to satisfy a physical hunger. I'm just putting all that food into a stomach that doesn't even want it, which, frankly, just makes me feel even more foolish about the whole thing. It's just... I'm eating without needing to eat, and I just can't seem to stop myself once I start, even though I know I'm not hungry.
Do you feel any sense of pleasure while eating during these episodes?

Pleasure? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't call it pleasure at all. I mean, I know what pleasure from food is supposed to feel like. My sister, Brenda, she makes this absolutely phenomenal strawberry rhubarb pie every Thanksgiving. She uses just the right amount of sugar so it's still got that tart bite to it, you know? And when I have a slice of that, sitting in her dining room with a cup of decaf coffee, that is pleasure. You savor a thing like that. You take a little bite with your fork and you think, 'Wow, this is truly delicious.' 

But this... what happens in the car after my Excel class? There's no savoring. There's no culinary appreciation whatsoever. Honestly, Doctor, I'm eating it so fast I barely even taste it half the time. It's just... chewing and swallowing, chewing and swallowing. Like a machine processing a stack of invoices. Just getting through the pile. 

Sometimes I'll buy these double cheeseburgers from the drive-thru, and you'd look at that and think, 'Well, Arthur, you must really love cheeseburgers to be buying three of them at once.' But I don't even really like them that much! The buns are usually a bit soggy from the steam in the wrapper, and the cheese is that highly processed stuff that just sort of glues itself to the roof of your mouth. But I just keep eating them anyway. It’s almost like the food is just... material. Just inventory to be moved. 

So, no, there’s no joy in it. No pleasure. It’s not some special treat I’m giving myself after a long day. If anything, it feels like work. It's just this frantic, messy task I feel compelled to get through before I can go home, throw the wrappers deep in the outside trash can so the neighbors don't see, and then face the guilt of it all. I almost wish it *were* pleasurable, because maybe then it would make a lick of sense on some basic human level, you know? Seeking pleasure is something you can put on a balance sheet. But doing this, getting no joy out of it, and feeling terrible afterward? It just completely defies reason.
Do you feel like you're trying to fill an emotional void when you eat after the class?

An emotional void? Gosh, I... I don't think so. That sounds a bit, well, a bit dramatic for someone like me, doesn't it? When I hear a phrase like 'emotional void,' I think of, oh, I don't know, a character in a Russian novel, or maybe someone on one of those afternoon talk shows. My sister Brenda watches those sometimes when she's doing her ironing, and they're always talking about 'filling the void' and 'healing your inner child' and all that sort of thing. But I just don't see myself in that language at all. 

If you look at my life, Doctor, it's really quite full. Not in a flashy way, mind you. I don't go skydiving or travel to Europe or anything extravagant. But I have my job at the firm, I have my routines, my Excel class at the community center, my Sunday mornings with the newspaper and the coffee... The ledger of my life is, well, it's balanced. I don't feel like there's some gaping hole in the middle of it all that needs patching up. 

I mean, if I had a void, wouldn't I feel it during the day? When I'm at the office tallying up the quarterly expenses for Mr. Henderson, or when I'm at the grocery store picking out my chicken breasts for the week? But I don't. I feel perfectly fine. Content, even. I like my quiet life. 

So when I'm in that drive-thru, it's not like I'm trying to shovel french fries into some big, dark, emotional black hole. It really isn't. Like I was trying to explain earlier with the emotions, there's just... nothing. No sadness, no emptiness, no void. It's just the driving, and the ordering, and the chewing. I really wish I could give you a better answer, because 'filling a void' sounds like a very neat, logical explanation, doesn't it? It sounds like something we could write down on a chart and figure out a step-by-step plan to fix. But if I'm being completely honest with you, and with myself, I just don't feel empty at all before I start eating. I just feel... bewildered by the whole routine, really.
Do you feel unfulfilled or dissatisfied with your daily routine or life in general?

Unfulfilled? Dissatisfied? Oh, my goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I know some people might look at a life like mine—fifty-five years old, working the same bookkeeping job for going on twenty years, taking a Tuesday night Excel class just to keep the skills sharp—and they might think, 'Well, Arthur, isn't that a bit dull?' But I don't find it dull in the slightest. I actually find a great deal of comfort in predictability. 

I like knowing that on Mondays, I review the payroll accounts for Mr. Henderson. I like knowing that on Thursdays, I go to the supermarket and buy my groceries for the week, always parking in the same section of the lot, if I can help it. It's... well, it's organized. It's neat. Everything has its proper place. I've never been one of those fellows who needs to be constantly entertained or, you know, chasing the next big thrill. I have my little apartment, I have my routines. On Sundays, I get the paper—the physical paper, mind you, none of this reading on a little glowing screen—and I sit in my armchair with a cup of coffee, and I do the crossword. And that, to me, is a perfectly fine way to spend a morning. I'm very satisfied with it, really. 

So when you ask if I'm unfulfilled, I really have to say no. The columns all add up. I have a roof over my head, a steady paycheck, a good relationship with my sister Brenda... I'm content. Which is exactly why this whole... this whole drive-thru business after my class is just so completely maddening! 

If I hated my job, or if I were miserable and lonely and wishing I had some grand, exciting life, well, then maybe I could understand why I'm sitting in my sedan eating three burgers in the dark. I could look at the situation and say, 'Ah, Arthur, you're unhappy with your daily lot, and that's why you're doing this.' It would be a logical cause and effect. But I'm *not* unhappy. I'm quite satisfied with my routine. I like my life exactly the way it is. So doing all this... it just doesn't make a lick of sense, Doctor. It really, truly doesn't.
Do you feel like you're doing something you don't want to be doing when you're eating after the class?

Oh, absolutely. That is... well, that is the crux of the whole bizarre situation, Doctor. It's exactly like doing something I don't want to be doing. I mean, it's not like I'm sleepwalking, you know? I'm completely awake. I'm sitting there, usually in the driver's seat, or sometimes I've brought the haul inside to the little table in my kitchen, and my brain is entirely aware of what's happening. I can see the clock on the microwave or the dashboard, I know I have to be up at 6:15 the next morning to get to the office, and my mind is just begging me to stop. 

I'll buy these things—sometimes it's the drive-thru, or sometimes I'll stop at the 24-hour pharmacy on the way back from the community center and get these big bags of chips or those little powdered donuts—and once I start on those snacks, I keep telling myself to close the bag and go to bed. I mean, I will literally have a full, rational conversation with myself in my head. I'll think, 'Arthur, just fold the top of the bag over. Put it down. Go inside, brush your teeth, and go to sleep.' It’s a very simple, logical directive. 

But... it's like there's a complete disconnect between management and the workers on the floor, if you catch my drift. I give the order to stop, but my hands just keep reaching for more. My brain says 'halt,' but my hand goes right back into the bag, pulls out another handful, and then I'm chewing and swallowing, and then the hand goes right back in again. I just sit there watching myself do it, completely unable to hit the brakes. It goes against every sensible bone in my body. 

And it just goes on and on like that until every last crumb is gone. And then... well, then the dust settles, and I just feel so terribly embarrassed and sick of myself. I sit there looking at the empty wrappers, feeling physically uncomfortable, of course, but mostly just sick with myself over the sheer lack of discipline. I think, 'You didn't even want to eat this, so why on earth did you just do it?' It's humiliating, really, to be a fifty-five-year-old man who can balance a million-dollar ledger but can't even tell his own hands to stop moving.
How often do these episodes of eating happen after your class?

How often? Well, let me think. The advanced Excel course—the one at the community center I was telling you about—runs for a full sixteen weeks. We started back in early September, right after Labor Day, when the weather was still quite warm. But this... this whole drive-thru and snacking business didn't start on day one. No, I'd say it's been going on for about the past three months. Right around the time we got into macros and VLOOKUPs, actually. Not that the coursework itself is stressing me out, you understand, I quite enjoy the formulas. But for about the past three months, it's become a rather grim little routine. 

It doesn't happen every single day, thank goodness. I don't think my checking account could handle that, let alone my pride. But there has usually been at least one night each week, almost always right after that class, when I overeat like that. I'll just completely lose control of the steering wheel, so to speak, and consume all those burgers or entire bags of donuts in one sitting. 

And... well. There is one other part of it, Doctor. Something I haven't quite brought myself to mention yet, because, frankly, it's the most shameful part of the whole equation. After I eat all of that, when the dust settles and I'm sitting there looking at the wrappers, feeling so dreadfully full and sick with myself... I go into the bathroom. And I... I make myself throw up afterward. 

I know, I know how it sounds. A man of my age, fifty-five years old, leaning over a toilet bowl. It's absolutely mortifying. But in that moment, my brain—the accountant in me, I suppose—just thinks, 'Arthur, you've made a terrible, glaring error on the ledger, and you have to erase it. You have to get it out and balance the books.' It feels like the only logical way to fix what I've just done. So, yes. At least once a week, for three months now. The driving, the eating, and then the... the getting rid of it. It's a terrible, exhausting cycle, it truly is.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start, even if you want to?

Yes, precisely. That is exactly what I was trying to get at a moment ago, Doctor. It is a complete and total inability to stop, even though every rational part of my brain is begging me to do just that. 

Like I was saying, once I start on those snacks—let's say it's those little powdered donuts from the 24-hour pharmacy, the ones in the crinkly white bags—it’s as if a switch just flips in my head. I'll have one, and then I keep telling myself, 'Alright Arthur, that's enough, just close the bag and go to bed.' I genuinely want to stop. I know I have to be at the bookkeeping firm early, I know I need my rest, and I certainly know I shouldn't be eating a week's worth of sugar at eleven o'clock at night. 

But... my hands just completely ignore the directive. They just keep reaching for more, over and over again. I'll be sitting there, getting powdered sugar all over my good slacks, literally having a conversation with myself about how much I want to stop, but the hand just goes into the bag, comes out, and I eat it. It just goes on and on like a machine until there is absolutely nothing left but crumbs at the bottom of the wrapper. 

And then, of course, the spell breaks, or whatever you want to call it, and I'm just left sitting there in the quiet of my car or my kitchen, feeling so incredibly embarrassed and sick of myself. Just utterly sick of myself for not having the simple, basic discipline to put a bag down when I wanted to. It's baffling.
Is there anything specific that happens right before you start eating after the class, like a thought, a feeling, or an event?

A thought or a feeling right before... hm. You know, Doctor, I've racked my brain about that very thing. Being a numbers man, I like to find the root of a discrepancy. I've tried to audit the whole evening, just go back through the ledger of my night line by line to see where the error originates. 

Class finishes at 8:30 PM sharp. The instructor—Mr. Henderson, nice fellow, used to work at a big logistics firm downtown—he wraps up the lecture, I pack my notes and my pens into my briefcase, and I walk out to the parking lot. It's usually quite quiet around the community center at that hour, maybe a few folks leaving the pottery class down the hall, but that's about it. I get into my sedan, put the key in the ignition, turn on the local news radio just low in the background, and I start the drive home. 

But as for a specific trigger? A sudden wave of sadness, or a spike of anxiety, or some... some sort of traumatic memory popping into my head? No. Nothing like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting there stewing over a bad day at the bookkeeping firm, or feeling particularly lonely, or anything dramatic. I might just be thinking about the nested formulas we just went over, or reminding myself that I need to pick up my slacks from the dry cleaner on Thursday, or wondering if I need to get my tires rotated soon because I thought I heard a little hum on the highway. 

Just completely ordinary, mundane, fifty-five-year-old man thoughts. There's no grand emotional shift. And then, before I know it, the steering wheel is just turning into the drive-thru lane or I'm pulling into the brightly lit parking lot of the pharmacy. It's almost frustrating how unremarkable the moments leading up to it are. I genuinely wish I could give you a clear cause and effect, you know, 'A happened, so B resulted,' because then I could just avoid 'A' altogether and balance the whole thing out. But no, I haven't noticed anything specific. I leave class, I drive, and then... well, the routine just begins.
Do you feel like you're losing control over your actions when you start eating after the class?

Yes, precisely. That's exactly it, Doctor. It really is a total loss of control, just like I was trying to describe with the powdered donuts a moment ago. It’s the most baffling, frustrating sensation. 

I’ll be sitting there—maybe I'm still in the driveway, or maybe I've made it inside to the kitchen counter under the fluorescent light—and once I start on those snacks... well, the rational part of my brain is fully awake, but I have absolutely zero authority over my own limbs. I keep telling myself, very clearly, 'Arthur, you need to close the bag right now. Just fold the top over, put a clip on it, and go to bed. You have the quarterly reports to review in the morning.' I genuinely, desperately want to stop. 

But my hands just keep reaching for more. They dip right back into the bag, pull out another piece, then another. I'm literally watching my own hands do it, completely ignoring my own internal instructions. It’s like the connection between my brain and my arms has just been severed, or like I'm a passenger in a vehicle where someone else has suddenly taken the steering wheel. I just keep going and going, completely on autopilot, until the food is completely gone. And then the fog lifts, and I'm just left standing there in the quiet, looking at the empty wrappers, feeling so profoundly embarrassed and sick of myself. It's a terrible, terrible feeling, being a mere spectator to your own actions like that.
Do you feel like you're punishing yourself when you eat after the class and then make yourself throw up?

Punishing myself? Well... I don't know if I'd use the word 'punishing,' Doctor. That implies a sort of... intentional malice toward myself, a desire to cause pain, and I don't think that's quite right. It's more about... well, it's about the consequences, you see. The physical reality of the situation. 

Being a bookkeeper, I deal in balances. In and out. Credits and debits. And when I sit there in my car or at the kitchen counter and I consume all those powdered donuts, or the entire sleeve of fig bars, or whatever it happens to be... well, that's a massive influx on the ledger, isn't it? A huge deposit of calories and sugar and fat. And my body... well, I'm fifty-five years old. My metabolism isn't what it was when I was playing junior varsity baseball back in high school. I sit at a desk all day crunching numbers, and then I sit in a classroom for two hours in the evening. I am entirely sedentary. 

So, when the fog lifts, and I see the empty wrappers, the sheer panic sets in. Not just the embarrassment I mentioned earlier, but a real, palpable fear. I think, 'Arthur, where is all this going to go?' It's going to go right to my waistline. It's going to show. I'll have to buy new slacks, my dress shirts will pull at the buttons when I'm sitting with a client... it'll be a visible, undeniable testament to my complete lack of self-control. People will look at me and they will know. 

And so... yes, a few times... actually, more than a few times recently... after those late-night eating spells, I have gone into the bathroom. I lock the door, turn on the fan—even though I live alone, it just feels necessary to have the noise—and I lean over the toilet and I make myself throw up. I just use my fingers. It's awful, it's undignified, and my eyes water terribly, but I just feel so incredibly scared that all that food will show on me. It's not a punishment, Doctor, it's... it's a desperate attempt to balance the books before the audit, if you understand my meaning. To just erase the transaction entirely so no one ever has to know it happened.
Do you think your eating habits after class are related to a deeper psychological issue?

A deeper psychological issue... well. I'm not a psychiatrist, Doctor, so I don't know if I'd use the word 'deeper,' as if it's some sort of repressed childhood memory or anything out of a movie. But... I suppose there is something fundamental about how I view myself that gets... derailed. Completely derailed. 

You see, I’ve been a bookkeeper for three decades. Precision, discipline, carefulness—those aren't just job requirements for me. That is who I am. I pride myself on being a man who has his house in order, someone who doesn't make sloppy mistakes. But... and this is the part that is so incredibly frustrating to admit... all of that pride, all of that identity, is completely fragile. It all hinges on my waistline. 

For example, I'll get up in the morning, shower, shave, and go to put on my clothes for work. If I put on my dress shirt and it feels even slightly tight around my middle... it just shatters me. It's not just a passing thought of, 'Oh, I should eat a salad for lunch.' No, it's a profound, overwhelming sense of defeat. On days my shirt feels tight around my middle, I feel like I have completely failed at being the careful, disciplined person I try so hard to be. It’s as if that one physical flaw negates everything else about my character. 

I can go into the office and do a brilliant job—the rest of my bookkeeping work can be absolutely flawless, not a single penny off in the ledgers, balancing accounts that would make a junior clerk weep—but it brings me no satisfaction. None at all. Because underneath my suit jacket, I know the shirt is pulling, and that tightness means I am undisciplined. It means I am a fraud. It's all I can think about while I'm sitting at my desk. So, if tying your entire sense of self-worth and morality to how your clothes fit is a psychological issue, then... yes. I suppose it very much is.
Do you feel like your eating after class is something you're ashamed of or something that makes you feel guilty, beyond just the physical consequences?

Oh, absolutely. The shame is... well, it's a very heavy thing to carry around, Doctor. It really is. It permeates just about everything, even if it hasn't completely stopped me in my tracks. 

Now, I want to be perfectly clear about one thing—I am not letting my actual responsibilities slip. I've always prided myself on my work ethic, you see. My bookkeeping at the firm? Still absolutely pristine. Not a single deadline missed, not a single decimal out of place on the ledgers. And my coursework for this evening class I'm taking—I'm still turning in all my assignments on time, keeping my grades right where they should be. I haven't let this... this whole situation ruin my actual performance or my livelihood. I am still getting all my work done.

But... well, the way I interact with the world around me? That's a different story entirely. It's taking a toll. A very significant toll. It used to be that after class, you know, a few of us would linger by the door, or walk out to the parking lot together under the streetlamps. There's a fellow named Gary, and a lovely woman, Susan, who usually sit in my row. We used to chat about the lecture, maybe complain a bit about the instructor's reading assignments—just normal, everyday banter. 

But lately... I just can't do it. The very second the instructor says we're dismissed, I am packing my briefcase as fast as humanly possible. I don't even make eye contact anymore. I just put my head down, mumble a quick 'goodnight,' and practically sprint out the door. Because all I can think about, for the entire last half hour of the lecture, is getting home. It's this overwhelming, buzzing preoccupation. I know what I'm going to do, I know the food is waiting, and I just feel so deeply ashamed of it even before it happens. 

I feel like if I stop and talk to Gary or Susan, they'll somehow look at me and see it in my eyes. They'll know what kind of pathetic routine I'm rushing off to do. So I avoid them completely. I've started leaving class so quickly, actively avoiding any casual time with my classmates, because the shame of what I'm about to do in my kitchen is just too loud in my head. I just need to get home and get it over with, and I can't bear the thought of anyone seeing me in that frantic state of mind. It's... well, it's quite lonely, to be perfectly honest, just rushing away from everyone like that.
Do you consider the eating episodes after class to be episodes of binge eating?

Crackers, chips, whatever I have in the cupboards. It’s... well, it’s honestly as if I am making up for the whole day. I've tried to audit the whole evening, just go back through the ledger of my night line by line to see where the error originates. 

Class finishes at 8:30 PM sharp. The instructor—Mr. Henderson, nice fellow, used to work at a big logistics firm downtown—he wraps up the lecture, I pack my notes and my pens into my briefcase, and I walk out to the parking lot. It's usually quite quiet around the community center at that hour, maybe a few folks leaving the pottery class down the hall, but that's about it. I get into my sedan, put the key in the ignition, turn on the local news radio just low in the background, and I start the drive home. 

But as for a specific trigger? A sudden wave of sadness, or a spike of anxiety, or some... some sort of traumatic memory popping into my head? No. Nothing like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting there stewing over a bad day at the bookkeeping firm, or feeling particularly lonely, or anything dramatic. I might just be thinking about the nested formulas we just went over, or reminding myself that I need to pick up my slacks from the dry cleaner on Thursday, or wondering if I need to get my tires rotated soon because I thought I heard a little hum on the highway. 

Just completely ordinary, mundane, fifty-five-year-old man thoughts. There's no grand emotional shift. And then, before I know it, the steering wheel is just turning into the drive-thru lane or I'm pulling into the brightly lit parking lot of the pharmacy. It's almost frustrating how unremarkable the moments leading up to it are. I genuinely wish I could give you a clear cause and effect, you know, 'A happened, so B resulted,' because then I could just avoid 'A' altogether and balance the whole thing out. But no, I haven't noticed anything specific. I leave class, I drive, and then... well, the routine just begins.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to a sense of loss of control
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're losing control over your actions when you start eating after the class?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those snacks, I keep telling myself to close the bag and go to bed, but my hands just keep reaching for more until I feel embarrassed and sick of myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking if the patient feels a loss of control over their actions when they start eating, which directly matches the Loss of Control symptom.

patient.answer:
Yes, precisely. That's exactly it, Doctor. It really is a total loss of control, just like I was trying to describe with the powdered donuts a moment ago. It’s the most baffling, frustrating sensation. 

I’ll be sitting there—maybe I'm still in the driveway, or maybe I've made it inside to the kitchen counter under the fluorescent light—and once I start on those snacks... well, the rational part of my brain is fully awake, but I have absolutely zero authority over my own limbs. I keep telling myself, very clearly, 'Arthur, you need to close the bag right now. Just fold the top over, put a clip on it, and go to bed. You have the quarterly reports to review in the morning.' I genuinely, desperately want to stop. 

But my hands just keep reaching for more. They dip right back into the bag, pull out another piece, then another. I'm literally watching my own hands do it, completely ignoring my own internal instructions. It’s like the connection between my brain and my arms has just been severed, or like I'm a passenger in a vehicle where someone else has suddenly taken the steering wheel. I just keep going and going, completely on autopilot, until the food is completely gone. And then the fog lifts, and I'm just left standing there in the quiet, looking at the empty wrappers, feeling so profoundly embarrassed and sick of myself. It's a terrible, terrible feeling, being a mere spectator to your own actions like that.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating episodes are related to a sense of punishment or self-criticism
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're punishing yourself when you eat after the class and then make yourself throw up?

target_item.name: Compensatory_Behavior_Purging
target_item.manifestation: A few times after those late-night eating spells, I have gone to the bathroom and made myself throw up because I was scared all that food would show on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's behavior of making himself throw up after eating, which corresponds to the purging compensatory behavior in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
Punishing myself? Well... I don't know if I'd use the word 'punishing,' Doctor. That implies a sort of... intentional malice toward myself, a desire to cause pain, and I don't think that's quite right. It's more about... well, it's about the consequences, you see. The physical reality of the situation. 

Being a bookkeeper, I deal in balances. In and out. Credits and debits. And when I sit there in my car or at the kitchen counter and I consume all those powdered donuts, or the entire sleeve of fig bars, or whatever it happens to be... well, that's a massive influx on the ledger, isn't it? A huge deposit of calories and sugar and fat. And my body... well, I'm fifty-five years old. My metabolism isn't what it was when I was playing junior varsity baseball back in high school. I sit at a desk all day crunching numbers, and then I sit in a classroom for two hours in the evening. I am entirely sedentary. 

So, when the fog lifts, and I see the empty wrappers, the sheer panic sets in. Not just the embarrassment I mentioned earlier, but a real, palpable fear. I think, 'Arthur, where is all this going to go?' It's going to go right to my waistline. It's going to show. I'll have to buy new slacks, my dress shirts will pull at the buttons when I'm sitting with a client... it'll be a visible, undeniable testament to my complete lack of self-control. People will look at me and they will know. 

And so... yes, a few times... actually, more than a few times recently... after those late-night eating spells, I have gone into the bathroom. I lock the door, turn on the fan—even though I live alone, it just feels necessary to have the noise—and I lean over the toilet and I make myself throw up. I just use my fingers. It's awful, it's undignified, and my eyes water terribly, but I just feel so incredibly scared that all that food will show on me. It's not a punishment, Doctor, it's... it's a desperate attempt to balance the books before the audit, if you understand my meaning. To just erase the transaction entirely so no one ever has to know it happened.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is related to a specific psychological disorder
doctor.question: Do you think your eating habits after class are related to a deeper psychological issue?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: On days my shirt feels tight around my middle, I feel like I have failed at being the careful, disciplined person I try to be, even if the rest of my bookkeeping work is fine.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about deeper psychological issues driving the eating habits, which provides the perfect opening to discuss how the patient's self-evaluation and sense of discipline are overly tied to his body weight and shape (the core psychological disturbance in Bulimia).

patient.answer:
A deeper psychological issue... well. I'm not a psychiatrist, Doctor, so I don't know if I'd use the word 'deeper,' as if it's some sort of repressed childhood memory or anything out of a movie. But... I suppose there is something fundamental about how I view myself that gets... derailed. Completely derailed. 

You see, I’ve been a bookkeeper for three decades. Precision, discipline, carefulness—those aren't just job requirements for me. That is who I am. I pride myself on being a man who has his house in order, someone who doesn't make sloppy mistakes. But... and this is the part that is so incredibly frustrating to admit... all of that pride, all of that identity, is completely fragile. It all hinges on my waistline. 

For example, I'll get up in the morning, shower, shave, and go to put on my clothes for work. If I put on my dress shirt and it feels even slightly tight around my middle... it just shatters me. It's not just a passing thought of, 'Oh, I should eat a salad for lunch.' No, it's a profound, overwhelming sense of defeat. On days my shirt feels tight around my middle, I feel like I have completely failed at being the careful, disciplined person I try so hard to be. It’s as if that one physical flaw negates everything else about my character. 

I can go into the office and do a brilliant job—the rest of my bookkeeping work can be absolutely flawless, not a single penny off in the ledgers, balancing accounts that would make a junior clerk weep—but it brings me no satisfaction. None at all. Because underneath my suit jacket, I know the shirt is pulling, and that tightness means I am undisciplined. It means I am a fraud. It's all I can think about while I'm sitting at my desk. So, if tying your entire sense of self-worth and morality to how your clothes fit is a psychological issue, then... yes. I suppose it very much is.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more characteristic of Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8) or Other Specified Sexual Dysfunction (F52.7) based on the presence of guilt or shame related to the eating episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel like your eating after class is something you're ashamed of or something that makes you feel guilty, beyond just the physical consequences?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still get my bookkeeping work and coursework done, but I have started leaving class quickly and avoiding casual time with classmates because I feel ashamed and preoccupied with getting home.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of shame or guilt regarding the eating behaviors, which directly relates to the patient's functional impairment manifestation where they describe avoiding casual time with classmates due to feeling ashamed.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. The shame is... well, it's a very heavy thing to carry around, Doctor. It really is. It permeates just about everything, even if it hasn't completely stopped me in my tracks. 

Now, I want to be perfectly clear about one thing—I am not letting my actual responsibilities slip. I've always prided myself on my work ethic, you see. My bookkeeping at the firm? Still absolutely pristine. Not a single deadline missed, not a single decimal out of place on the ledgers. And my coursework for this evening class I'm taking—I'm still turning in all my assignments on time, keeping my grades right where they should be. I haven't let this... this whole situation ruin my actual performance or my livelihood. I am still getting all my work done.

But... well, the way I interact with the world around me? That's a different story entirely. It's taking a toll. A very significant toll. It used to be that after class, you know, a few of us would linger by the door, or walk out to the parking lot together under the streetlamps. There's a fellow named Gary, and a lovely woman, Susan, who usually sit in my row. We used to chat about the lecture, maybe complain a bit about the instructor's reading assignments—just normal, everyday banter. 

But lately... I just can't do it. The very second the instructor says we're dismissed, I am packing my briefcase as fast as humanly possible. I don't even make eye contact anymore. I just put my head down, mumble a quick 'goodnight,' and practically sprint out the door. Because all I can think about, for the entire last half hour of the lecture, is getting home. It's this overwhelming, buzzing preoccupation. I know what I'm going to do, I know the food is waiting, and I just feel so deeply ashamed of it even before it happens. 

I feel like if I stop and talk to Gary or Susan, they'll somehow look at me and see it in my eyes. They'll know what kind of pathetic routine I'm rushing off to do. So I avoid them completely. I've started leaving class so quickly, actively avoiding any casual time with my classmates, because the shame of what I'm about to do in my kitchen is just too loud in my head. I just need to get home and get it over with, and I can't bear the thought of anyone seeing me in that frantic state of mind. It's... well, it's quite lonely, to be perfectly honest, just rushing away from everyone like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is more aligned with Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8) or Other Specified Sexual Dysfunction (F52.7) by inquiring about the presence of binge eating as a primary symptom
doctor.question: Do you consider the eating episodes after class to be episodes of binge eating?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: Once I start on those snacks, I keep telling myself to close the bag and go to bed, but my hands just keep reaching for more until I feel embarrassed and sick of myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient considers their eating episodes to be 'binge eating'. Binge eating involves a loss of control over eating, which matches the S050 symptom profile where the patient describes an inability to stop eating once they start.

patient.answer:
Binge eating... well, I suppose that’s the word for it, isn't it? It sounds so dramatic, like something you'd hear on a television program, but... if I really sit down and analyze the mechanics of what happens when I get home, maybe it is. 

Because the truth is, the moment I walk through the front door, I set my briefcase down by the hall table—always in the exact same spot, mind you, right next to the mail tray—and I go straight to the kitchen. The house is completely quiet, just the hum of the refrigerator. And I open the pantry. 

And once I start on those snacks... it's like a switch flips. A complete mechanical failure. I’ll open a bag of something, and I keep telling myself, the entire time I'm chewing, 'Arthur, just have a handful. Close the bag. Put the clip back on it and go to bed. You have work in the morning.' I am literally having this rational conversation in my head, pleading with myself to just stop and go to sleep. 

But my hands... it's as if they don't even belong to me anymore. They just keep reaching for more, over and over, dipping back into the bag or the box, almost on autopilot. I can't seem to physically halt the motion, even though my brain is begging me to quit. I just keep reaching and reaching, chewing and swallowing, until I feel completely, profoundly embarrassed. I just sit there in the quiet kitchen, looking at the crumbs, and I feel so entirely sick of myself. Sick of my complete lack of willpower. So, if that total inability to stop myself once I've started is what you mean by a binge... then yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly what it is.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's behavior is consistent with a diagnosis of Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.8) or an Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F52.7)
doctor.question: Do you believe your eating habits after class are a significant departure from your usual eating habits and are causing you significant distress?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that after my evening class I sometimes stop for food and end up eating a full fast-food meal, candy from the vending machine, and then more snacks at home like I am making up for the whole day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the eating habits involve consuming a significantly larger amount of food than usual, which directly relates to the symptom of eating a large amount.

patient.answer:
A departure? Oh, heavens, yes. It is night and day, Doctor. A complete and utter inversion of how I operate during my normal waking hours. You see, during the workday, I am very measured. A sensible breakfast, a modest lunch at my desk—everything accounted for, everything strictly monitored. 

But what actually brought me in here to see you—what finally made me pick up the telephone and make this appointment—is the sheer, baffling volume of what happens after that evening class. It is so far outside my normal character that it frightens me. 

I’ll leave the campus, and instead of just taking my usual, direct route home... I take a detour. I'll pull into a drive-thru and order a full fast-food meal. And I mean the entire combination—the burger, the large fries, the heavy soda. I'll eat it right there in the car on the way back. But it doesn't stop there, and that is where the distress really sets in. I'll get to my building, and before I even go up to my apartment, I will literally stop at the vending machine in the lobby and buy candy. Two or three heavy, sugary candy bars, and I'll eat those on the elevator ride up to my floor. 

And *then*, as I was telling you just a moment ago, I walk through my front door, put my briefcase down by the mail tray, and go straight into the kitchen for even more snacks. Crackers, chips, whatever I have in the cupboards. It’s... well, it’s honestly as if I am making up for the whole day. Like my brain just decides that because I was so rigidly disciplined for the first fourteen hours of the day, I suddenly need to consume an entire day's worth of food in the span of forty-five minutes. 

So, yes, it is a massive, shocking departure from my usual careful nature. And the distress... well, it's immense. To watch yourself behave so completely out of character, to consume all of that when you know better... it's exhausting. It's exactly why I'm sitting here in this chair right now, because I just cannot keep living with this nightly collapse of my discipline.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of recurring episodes of eating large quantities of food in a short period, feeling a lack of control during these episodes, and experiencing significant distress and guilt afterward are consistent with the diagnostic criteria for Other Eating Disorders, specifically binge eating disorder.
